blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — prescription icosapent ethyl versus nonprescription fish oil
stem: An adult with severe hypertriglyceridemia is prescribed icosapent ethyl. Which teaching is most accurate?

options.A: Icosapent ethyl is a standardized prescription EPA product; nonprescription fish-oil supplements have variable fatty-acid content and should not be substituted as dose-for-dose equivalents.
options.B: A nonprescription fish-oil supplement can replace icosapent ethyl dose for dose because omega-3 supplements have standardized EPA content and equivalent prescription evidence.
options.C: Icosapent ethyl is used mainly for its antihypertensive effect and has little expected triglyceride-lowering activity when prescribed for severe hypertriglyceridemia.
options.D: Icosapent ethyl contains both EPA and DHA, so the DHA component and a resulting LDL-C increase are required features of its triglyceride-lowering mechanism.

rationale: Current FDA labeling identifies icosapent ethyl as a prescription ethyl ester of eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) indicated as an adjunct to diet to reduce triglycerides in adults with severe hypertriglyceridemia. The 2026 ACC/AHA dyslipidemia guideline states that icosapent ethyl contains EPA only and that nonprescription fish-oil supplements are not equivalent to prescription omega-3 medications and have variable fatty-acid content. Therefore A is correct. B makes an unsafe equivalence, C misstates the therapeutic purpose, and D incorrectly describes an EPA/DHA product rather than icosapent ethyl.
educational_objective: Distinguish prescription icosapent ethyl from nonprescription fish-oil supplements: it is a standardized EPA medication with defined dosing and evidence, and OTC products are not dose-for-dose equivalents.
